query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron during alloy synthesis will promote boron segregation at the internal lamellar colony boundaries, thereby strengthening these interfaces and mitigating microcrack initiation, which in turn improves both the strength and the room‐temperature tensile ductility of the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack nucleation during room-temperature deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small (trace) concentration of boron into the alloy melt during processing so that boron will preferentially segregate to the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: The processing must maintain the dual-phase lamellar microstructure (i.e., lamella spacing and phase volume fractions) and be controlled such that the boron level is low enough to avoid forming brittle boride precipitates. The alloy should be evaluated under room-temperature tensile loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion at the internal boundaries due to boron segregation.
generation.mechanism: Boron is expected to segregate to the high-energy interphase boundaries in the lamellar colonies, lowering the interfacial free energy and increasing cohesion. This strengthened interface reduces stress concentration during tensile loading and delays microcrack nucleation, which permits more uniform plastic deformation and contributes to increased yield strength without sacrificing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated eutectic high-entropy alloys, the boron-doped alloy is predicted to show a higher yield strength and an increased elongation-to-failure during room-temperature tensile tests, evidencing simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies processed without any interfacial modification, typically exhibiting early microcrack initiation and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention is beneficial only if the boron concentration is optimized: too little may not sufficiently strengthen the interfaces, while too much could lead to the formation of brittle boride phases. The effect is anticipated to hold under ambient temperature tensile testing, while different temperature regimes or loading conditions may yield different results.
generation.uncertainty: The precise boron concentration needed to maximize interfacial strengthening without inducing deleterious secondary phases is not known. Further, the long-term stability of the boron-enriched interfaces under cyclic or complex loading remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one set with an optimized trace boron addition and one control set without boron. Use TEM/EDS to confirm the presence and distribution of boron at the lamellar colony boundaries. Then, perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests and compare yield strengths, ultimate tensile strengths, and elongation-to-failure of the modified versus unmodified alloys.
measurements: TEM/EDS mapping of interfaces to verify boron segregation
Room-temperature tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation to failure)
Fractography via SEM to assess microcrack initiation sites and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and tensile elongation (e.g., improvements with p < 0.05) relative to the control, or if brittle boride phases are observed in the microstructure that degrade either strength or ductility, then the hypothesis is falsified.
